newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Germany seeks to dispel fears of Asia jobs drain.
newsitem.headline: Germany seeks to dispel fears of Asia jobs drain.

text.p: Germany's economics minister on Thursday sought to allay concerns that Europe's biggest economy was rapidly losing jobs to Asia, saying corporate success abroad would help ease a jobs crisis at home.

German Economy Minister Guenter Rexrodt made the comment during a trade visit to Australia, where German industrial giant Siemens AG has emerged as a major employer with plans to become a commercial force in the Asia-Pacific.
Other German companies are also racing to build a permanent presence in the region's briskly growing economies, helping to build power plants, factories and telecommunication networks.

"Siemens is a pacemaker and we are very proud of that," Rexrodt said before planting a tree at the site of the company's new Australasian headquarters in Melbourne. Siemens employs over 2,300 people in Australia and New Zealand.
"But on the other hand there are question marks. What happens if all of the new jobs are created outside of Germany?"

Rexrodt answered his own question, saying German success abroad, especially in the emerging economies of Asia, was crucial to easing unemployment at home, where the jobless rate has climbed to a post-World War Two high of 10.9 percent.
"Three new jobs out of Germany keep or create one new job in Germany," Rexrodt said.
Germany's jobs crisis is widely expected to receive another blow later on Thursday, when jobless data for January is due to be released.
Rexrodt suggested that success in overseas markets was only part of the solution and said greater inward investment was also needed to create jobs, especially in the old East Germany.

"We don't have a problem with German companies investing in Asia or wherever. We have a problem that...for the time-being there are only a few foreign companies who invest in Germany," Rexrodt told reporters.

Rexrodt, who arrived in Australia from New Zealand on Wednesday, is heading a delegation of about 40 German business leaders on a week-long trade mission aimed as much at attracting job-creating investment as snaring local contracts.

"We would especially invite companies to do business in the new states in the former East Germany because this area is a bridge for additional activities to eastern and middle-eastern Europe," Rexrodt said.

The minister said reforms aimed at boosting investment and putting the country's four million jobless back to work, were already well underway, citing a tax relief package designed to cut German taxes to their lowest levels in since World War Two.
But he said more needed to be done, especially in Germany's "fixed" labour market.

"We need more flexibility and this means we have to have, between the unions and employers, new kinds of contracts," Rexrodt said, adding contracts should be tailored to the special circumstances of each company and region.
